newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Key Taleban town falls, another hit-Afghan sources.
newsitem.headline: Key Taleban town falls, another hit-Afghan sources.

text.p: Forces of the ousted Afghan government have taken the front-line headquarters of the Islamic Taleban and launched an assault on another town on the road south to Kabul, reliable Afghan sources said on Sunday.
They said Jabal-os-Siraj at the mouth of the Salang Pass through the Hindu Kush mountains fell on Saturday night and Charikar, a 30-minute drive to the south, came under attack on Sunday morning.

The reported fall of Jabal-os-Siraj is a major setback for the Taleban, who pursued ousted military chief Ahmad Shah Masood north after taking Kabul just two weeks ago and bottled up his forces in the Panjsher Valley, which begins near the town.

They were unable to penetrate the narrow gorge into the Panjsher, and on Tuesday Masood launched a counter-attack in the Salang Pass, then orchestrated a series of guerrilla strikes well behind the Taleban front-lines.
"Yes, Jabal-os-Siraj has fallen. It fell on Saturday evening," one reliable source told Reuters. "They attacked Charikar early this morning."
The Taleban in Kabul have denied strenuously reports that Jabal-os-Siraj, their front-line headquarters for both the Salang and Panjsher Valley fronts, had fallen.
But the sources said Taleban forces had retreated from Jabal-os-Siraj to Charikar, a 30-minute drive to the south, and that town was under attack on Sunday morning.
The status of the town was not immediately known and the sources said they could not confirm reports it had fallen.

Mostly ethnic Tajik forces loyal to Masood, military chief to ousted President Burhanuddin Rabbani, have struck in and around Charikar over the last three days. Reporters heard heavy small arms fire there on Saturday.

People in the mostly Tajik town said earlier in the week the largely ethnic Pushtun Taleban had been rounding up young men suspected to be fomenting opposition to the militia and driving them away to an unknown destination.
Masood's commanders have said the people of the town joined in the fight against the Taleban and it was expected to fall soon.

The charismatic Masood, who won a reputation as an outstanding guerilla general in the 1980s when the Soviet army backed a communist government in Kabul, has also orchestrated guerrilla attacks even nearer Kabul.
Late on Saturday, the main road north remained cut about 15 km (nine miles) north of the Kabul valley.
Taleban forces going to and from Charikar, a 90-minute drive from Kabul, had to take a looping side-road that joins the main highway just south of Charikar.

Masood's forces have also struck at Bagram, Kabul's main airbase some 50 km (30 miles) north of the city, and the Taleban have responded with bombing raids on suspected Masood positions in the village of Bagram next to the base, witnesses said.
The attacks appear to have confined the Taleban to the roads, as Masood organised strikes reminiscent of his tactics in the 1980s.
They have disconcerted Taleban fighters, who struck back at the attackers near Kabul with tank fire and multiple rocket launchers.
The Taleban said on Saturday the attacks had been contained and pointed to smoking houses of people whom they said had led attacks against the Islamic militia.

But, in sharp contrast to genial conversations with reporters earlier in the week, Taleban fighters on the road have become aggressive, beating two reporters on Saturday and smashing a television camera.
Veteran Afghan watchers in Kabul said that was a sign the tide had turned against the Taleban north of Kabul.

But they said it was unlikely Masood would be able to retake the city without the backing of northern Uzbek leader Abdul Rashid Dostum, who signed a miltiary pact with the Tajik chief earlier this week, promising to help him unless fighting stopped.
The Afghan sources said that so far, there had been no sign of Dostum's forces being involved in the fighting in the Salang Pass, which he mostly controls.
